part.title: Beginning!
part.setting: The Day of the Breach, continued.

Hundreds of them stood still in the golden light, heads tilted, as if they heard a far-off song. "They look," said
slowly, "as though somebody has just let go of them."
It lasted a few minutes. Then a crack ran across the northern sky, and every Ender's eyes blazed red.
Now a hand has taken hold again, harder than before.
Thirty Enders came down the street in a pack. Layla fired, but there were too many. "Layla!" called Fanny. "Fire along my line."
It was the "please" that did it. Fanny had never said it before.
A silver cable glowed violet across the street, charged with Fanny's own energy. Layla laid her cannon along it. Her core and Fanny's hummed like two strings tuned to one note. She fired.
The beam did not go straight. It followed the cable. It looped round one Ender's legs, through the next one's chest, over a third one's shoulder. It took eleven.

Fanny held out her hand. Layla took it. A spark of teal and violet jumped between their palms. Layla had never held anyone's hand before.
In the hold of the ship,

Pip tore the cables from the chair and tangled them round the guards' knees. Ruby sprang free. They ran for the ramp, with the
Corvin reached the hatch first. He pushed Ruby gently down the ramp. Then he turned and locked both hands on the Warden's wrists. It was ten times as strong. He did not give way.

"Miss Ruby," he said. "I have been a soldier all my life. I fought on four worlds and never knew why. It is strange to find, at the end, that one has a reason. It is an honour to be a soldier for something."
He pulled. The hull above the hatch split, and gold fire swelled. The Warden fell down the hill.
had turned back to help, because she was a medic. She lay under a slab of metal. She was dead.
She wanted to see the sun,
I said I would show her.

Corvin was still alive, with his chest torn open. He looked up at the sky. "It's warm," he whispered. "It is a great deal better than the lamps. Go, madam. She will need you. She does not know it. But she will."
His golden eyes went dark. Pip, crying, pulled Ruby to her feet. Pip had lived. Ruby took up her scythe and ran north.

On a plain of red dust at the edge of the city, a gold giant came out of the smoke. A red gem as big as a door burned on its brow. It raised its arms, and a beam as wide as a street tore up the ground.

Fanny flew at it, zigzagging, with her wings spread. She flew into a spiral of gold light, and the sky went white. When Layla could see again, Fanny was beside her on a ridge, singed and breathing hard. "Now," said Fanny. "It's the head."

A violet thread ran from their feet to the red gem. Layla laid her cannon along it and fired. The beam met the giant's gold light in the sky. A huge white flash filled the plain and swallowed two girls, tumbling hand in hand.
At the lower end of the ward,
guarded a shelter under a fallen steel bridge. Two young cadets stood with him.
A rose-coloured wedge came down out of the sunset: a few hundred
girls with pink eyes. At their head walked
hanging from her collar. The cadets charged. One small ball of magenta fire threw them both down the bank.
Then a flash of dark blue swept in. Legion soldiers burst apart in sparks. Ruby stood among them, panting. "Angela," she said, holding out her open hand. "Angela, stop!"
Angela attacked. Ruby parried again and again. She could not strike back. She had made that face herself. A blow threw her onto the wreck of the bridge. Angela stood over her, calm and cold.
Ruby got up. "I'm Ruby," she said. "Don't you remember? We've been together since the very beginning."
She remembered the bay of cyan light where she had built Angela from scrap. She had been afraid it would hurt, and she had asked,
Angela had opened her blue eyes.
She remembered the secret garden at the top of the
, and a beam of sun. Angela had lifted her hand into the light.
She had held out her other hand, shining with joy. And Ruby, afraid, had turned away for one moment. She had wished every hour since that she had not.
"I don't want you to be like this," Ruby said, and her voice cracked. "I don't want freedom at the cost of you! Wake up, Angela!"
A crystal shard flew past her ear. It was Angela's answer.
Ruby dropped her scythe. "How did we end up like this?" she said. She ran straight at Angela and threw both arms round her.
On the red plain, in the dusk, Layla and Fanny stood back to back. Enders closed in from every side. Far off, a shape as tall as a tower still stood against the last light.
Layla felt Fanny's back against hers, and the small hard knock of a heart.
They stood on a grey quay in the late afternoon. Behind them lay the harbour. Before them ran the long white Embankment, and the city was going to pieces.
"After you," said Vexana, and raised her staff.
came over the sea-wall at a run. It was long and black, with gold-edged plates and a face like a skull. It bounded straight at Guinevere. She did not move.
Twelve paces behind her, in the shadow of a crane, Vexana sang one low note. It came from the staff itself. A small bolt of violet fire shot across the quay and struck the Ender in the eye.
The Ender froze in mid-leap. Guinevere hit it in the chest. It burst into black and gold cinders.
"I froze it," said Vexana. Her hands were shaking. "I have always heard them hum. If you sing the opposite note, they stop. For about a second."
"That's all we need!" Guinevere grinned. "Come on, then! I've got a partner!"
They fought for forty-one minutes. Guinevere never looked back. She knew exactly where Vexana stood.

In the twenty-ninth minute, the note changed. A small dark bead fell from the black orb. It was no bigger than a plum. Where it touched the quay, three Enders folded into a point as small as a coin, and were gone.
"Sorry," said Vexana's voice, very fast. "I haven't practised that one."
We shall talk about that later,

In the thirty-fifth minute, an Ender hit her from the side. She fell on the wet stone. For the first time that day, the staff stopped singing. Boots ran across the quay. It was not in the plan. A white-gloved hand came down in front of her face.
Then Vexana ran back to the crane, and the staff began to sing again.
In the thirty-eighth minute, Guinevere's star blazed at her collar. She had never seen it so bright. "I can feel you!" she shouted.
"I know! Mine too! We're the same note! I can hear you thinking!"
It was true. Guinevere felt a clean light in her, from her head to her boots.
A thin rope of silver and gold sprang up between her star and the staff, across twelve paces of smoke. In the command room, far away,
cried that the score was off the scale. They did not hear her.
. Angela did not hold her back. In Ruby's arms, her eyes faded slowly from magenta to grey.
Ruby heard a small ticking in the girl's chest.
She laid her cheek on the peach hair.
"I think I know what hurt means now," she said. "I'm... hurting." She had never said it to anyone. "How do I stop it? If it wasn't for all of this!"
She wept. After a long time, she felt a small stir.

A red line ran along the visor. A cold, clean tide came into her, and her tears dried.
said something that was not herself.

She laid Angela gently on the rubble and stood. Her left eye, which was blue with a white star, had turned red. She took up her scythe. Five Legion soldiers came at her. She shut her eyes and killed them all, without joy.
Then she walked towards the shelter.
stood in her way with his arms spread. "Ruby," he said. "You were crying. You wouldn't."
She swung the flat of the scythe, and it threw him against a barrel. Behind the barrel crouched a small barefoot girl in a white nightdress. "No," the child whispered.
Deep inside, Angela was in a grey place. Nothing hurt there, and nothing mattered.
Then a small cry reached her.
It meant that someone was needed.
said a voice from long ago.
The grey cracked. She saw the cyan bay. She saw the garden, and a hand held up to the sun.
Her eyes lit blue. On her shoulder,
"Deploying," said Angela, in a cracked voice. "Shield."

A ring of gold-pink light rose from the ground, with two pointed ears on top like a cat's. It swept under the falling blade and lifted the child into the air. The scythe stopped a hand's breadth from her hair.
At that moment, the sky cracked.
A silver line ran across the sky, and a cold pale light fell on the ship on the hill. The
shattered into gold dust. The crystal on the Marshal's baton went with it.

In the northern ward, Ruby's eye turned blue again. She remembered everything. She had watched it all from behind her own face. The scythe fell from her hands.
The shield set the child down, and she ran to her mother. Tetra dropped into Angela's hands, with a crack across his head. Angela reached out. "I think I was gone. Will you stay?"
crept down the slope and put one long arm round them both. "I'm still here," he said. "I'll mend things."
That was how they were found.

heard the same voice. It came from the north, in a long, cold wave. In the forty-first minute, the Enders stopped where they stood. Their blades went down. Then they turned and filed away along the Embankment.
It was a woman's voice, cool and very tired. Guinevere felt a strange pity.
"Guin," said Vexana. She was white and shaking. "I heard it. I understood it. It's her. The one the Core cannot bind."
"I could feel her. I think she heard." Vexana put her hand over her star. "Us. The note went right up into the sky. I think she heard us."
Guinevere took her by the shoulders. "Look at me. It's over. We won. We're alive."
Vexana looked at the small, sooty, grinning face. Slowly, her own face loosened.
"We held the harbour for forty-one minutes!" said Guinevere. "
said it was a record!" She threw up both fists. "We're the best partners in the
Vexana laughed. She put back her head and shouted it too. "The best! In the whole of the world!"
Their voices went out across the burning water, one high and one low.
In the command room, Chang'e stared at a screen. The beacon that followed the Core had gone dark. "I think the Will has recalled it."
stood at her shoulder, a hand on her chest. "Recalled," she said softly. "By a command it can't refuse."
"Yes," said Chang'e gently, after a long look. "I imagine it's rather like that."
I am glad that you were not harmed.
Armoured guards led Ruby and Angela into a vehicle bay at the foot of the tower. They were not bound.
On the third floor, Layla and Fanny watched on a monitor. Both were filthy.
"So that's the enemy," said Layla. "They don't look like much."
Looks like we got a few newcomers,
sat by the dark window, with her arm in a sling.

Later, a very small scientist brought a flask of tea to the room where Ruby sat. "I'm Chang'e," she said. "It's tea, with a great deal of sugar. It's what we do where I come from, when someone's had a bad time."
Ruby had been taught that a gift was a debt. She drank. It was far too sweet. It was the best thing she had ever tasted.
"I'm afraid I shall have to keep that," said Chang'e, touching the dead visor. "It's finished talking. But I should like to take out whatever answered."
Ruby took it off herself. "Will it hurt?"
A tear ran down Ruby's cheek and fell into the cup.
That night Layla and Fanny sat on a roof above the ruins, instead of going home to sleep.
"We'd probably get along," said Layla gruffly, "if you weren't so competitive."

"I could say the same of you," said Fanny. After a while she said quietly, "I have an elder brother. I've wanted to fight beside him since I was small. But he went to the front, and I had to stay. Maybe one day I'll be good enough to stand beside him."
She wasn't trying to put me down,
She was only trying to catch up.

She stood up and held out her hand. "All rested up? If so, let's get back to our training! We'll get stronger. And you'll stand beside your brother. I'll be on the other side of you, with the biggest gun he's ever seen."
Fanny began to smile. She took the hand and let herself be pulled up.
"We're the protectors of all humanity," they said together.
It was not an ending. It was only the first morning of the longest day.
